notes: Owns comments inside the source: a comment that restates the code, a missing why-comment (intent, rationale, a non-obvious constraint or workaround), an interface comment on a routine or type that says what a caller needs and the signature does not, a comment that contradicts or has drifted from the code it describes, commented-out code and TODO or FIXME markers (signals commented_out_code and todo_marker), and following the language's documented doc-comment convention. Yields documents outside the source (README, design documents, generated reference sites) to documentation-beyond-comments; identifier naming, including the choice of a long name over a short name plus a comment, to naming-identifiers; comment placement and spacing to layout-and-coding-style; stating a precondition or invariant as a checkable contract to contracts-assertions-and-invariants; deprecation notices to api-evolution-and-deprecation. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust; a doc-comment syntax (Javadoc tags, docstring layout, rustdoc sections, Go doc paragraphs) is named as 'the language's documented doc-comment convention' and appears in an Example only. Contested: in johnousterhout/aposd-vs-clean-code README.md, sections 'Comments' and 'Comments Summary', John Ousterhout (A Philosophy of Software Design) holds that missing comments cost more than bad ones and that interfaces and abstractions cannot be defined without many comments, while Robert C. Martin (Clean Code) holds that comments as generally practiced are a net negative and that their information should be recast into code, for example longer names, where possible; both agree there that implementation code needs comments only where it is non-obvious.

notes: Owns the use of variables and data inside a routine: declaration close to first use and initialization at declaration, the narrowest scope and the shortest live time, one purpose per variable, shadowing, global variables, magic numbers versus named constants (signal magic_number), and the numeric pitfalls of the fundamental types: integer overflow and wraparound, integer division and lossy narrowing conversions, floating-point equality and accumulated rounding, binary floating point for decimal quantities such as money. Yields identifier naming (CC11) to naming-identifiers; shared mutable state between components and immutability as a design choice to mutable-state-and-immutability; strings as text and character encoding to internationalization-and-text-encoding; the ownership and lifetime of what a pointer or reference holds to resource-management-and-ownership; domain types over primitives to domain-modeling-and-domain-language. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust; numeric semantics differ by language (Python integers do not overflow, TypeScript numbers are binary floating point, Rust panics on overflow in debug builds, Java and Go wrap), so a numeric rule states the condition under which it holds, and a rule true in one language only belongs elsewhere. Numerical-methods and algorithm research, low-latency numeric tuning, and a global read and written from several threads (concurrency correctness) are reserved specialties outside the topic.

notes: Owns the flow of control inside a routine: ordering straight-line code so its dependencies are visible, conditionals (the normal case first, complete if-else chains, a switch's default case and fallthrough), loops (one entry and a clear exit, loop-control variables, off-by-one bounds, one job per loop body), unusual control structures (early return and guard clauses, recursion with a base case and bounded depth, goto and labelled jumps), boolean expressions (simplified, stated positively, never compared with boolean literals), nesting depth (signal deep_nesting), and cyclomatic or cognitive complexity per routine. Yields routine length to routine-size-and-parameters; replacing a conditional chain with a lookup table or an explicit state machine, and exhaustive dispatch over an enumerated state set, to table-driven-and-state-machines; the local handling of a failure and exceptions used as control flow to error-and-exception-handling; a loop rewritten as a pipeline to functional-style-and-pipelines; replacing a type switch with polymorphism to the design group (inheritance-versus-composition, design-patterns-in-construction); loop performance to profiling-and-code-tuning. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust; a construct only some of them have (goto exists only in Go, switch falls through by default only in Java and TypeScript) appears in an Example only. Asynchronous and concurrent control flow is reserved to the concurrency-correctness specialty.

Yields the form of an individual conditional, a switch's default and fallthrough, and nesting to control-flow; tables moved into external configuration files to runtime-configuration; the State design pattern's class structure to design-patterns-in-construction; lexers and parsers driven by tables or grammars to parsing-and-grammar-based-input. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust; an exhaustiveness mechanism only some languages have (sealed types, match exhaustiveness, a never-typed check) appears in an Example only, and where a language has no exhaustiveness check the rule states the runtime default it needs. A state machine shared between threads is reserved to concurrency correctness, and protocol state machines across services belong to distributed systems, outside the corpus.

notes: Owns the contract as part of an interface: preconditions a caller must meet, postconditions the routine guarantees, invariants a type establishes in its constructor and preserves across every public operation, loop invariants where a loop's correctness is not obvious, assertions as executable statements of conditions that must hold and never of expected failures, assertions free of side effects, the fact that assertions may be disabled in production (Python under -O, Java without -ea, Rust debug_assert in release builds), and the substitutability rule for subtypes (a precondition no stronger, a postcondition no weaker). notes: Owns changing a published interface without breaking its callers: what counts as a breaking change (removing or renaming an element, changing a signature, strengthening a precondition or weakening a postcondition, changing observable behaviour that callers depend on, per Hyrum's Law), signalling a breaking change through the version number (semantic versioning's major version), additive evolution (a new optional parameter, an options type, room left for new variants and fields), and deprecation before removal: mark the element with the language's deprecation mechanism, name the replacement in the notice, keep it working for a stated period, warn at the caller's site, migrate the callers, then remove; and adding no new use of a deprecated element. Yields the choice, pinning and upgrading of third-party dependencies to dependency-management; codebase-wide migrations of callers to large-scale-changes-and-migrations; the first design of an API's shape to api-design-and-use; the contract rules under subtyping to contracts-assertions-and-invariants. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust; a deprecation mechanism (@Deprecated, #[deprecated], warnings.warn with DeprecationWarning, the 'Deprecated:' doc-comment paragraph, the @deprecated JSDoc tag) is named in an Example only. Versioning of wire protocols and service APIs belongs to distributed systems, and release and team process to process management, both outside the corpus.
